newsitem.title: UK: FORECAST - UK Feb input prices to feel stg benefit.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST - UK Feb input prices to feel stg benefit.

text.p: Falling oil prices and a rising pound will exert a downward drag on input prices in February, but higher commodity costs will partially offset that pressure, economists said.

On balance the data, due at 0930 GMT on Monday, will reinforce a picture of muted pipeline inflation in Britain, laying to rest any lingering doubts about the need for an early tightening in monetary policy.
A Reuter poll of analysts showed expectations for a 0.1 percent seasonally-adjusted fall in input prices in February but a 0.4 percent rise in non-adjusted output prices.
The annual rate for output prices is forecast to fall to 1.2 percent from 1.5 percent in January, with input prices ticking up slightly to minus 5.9 percent from minus 6.3 percent.
Ciaran Barr, UK economist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell, said the strength of the pound would again be reflected in February's input prices.
"The main theme is sterling," he said. "It takes time to feed through."
Sterling has gained around 16 percent on a trade-weighted basis since the summer of last year.

With the latest Purchasing Managers survey showing a decline in the price index to its lowest level since July, coupled with a hefty drop in oil prices, Barr said he expected a 0.7 percent fall in input prices on the month, bringing the annual rate to minus 6.7 percent.
But economists said the dampening effects of the rallying pound and declining oil price may well be balanced out by stronger non-oil commodity prices.
Higher metal and imported food prices would prevent any significant softening in input price inflation, they said.
After a fall in the core measure of output prices in January to a 30-year low, analysts said the decline would slow somewhat in February's numbers.
Jonathan Loynes at HSBC Markets said that while he expected the core rate to hold at 0.7 percent in February, growth could slow to 0.5 percent in the months ahead.
"The latest monthly trends survey from the CBI (Conferedation of British Industry) held out the prospect of even lower core output price inflation," he said.

Economists said the sluggish state of Britain's manufacturing sector would ensure any output price pressure would remain limited, although they did not expect manufacturers to pass the full reduction in costs through to retailers.
Keith Edmonds, chief analyst at IBJ International, said he too saw sterling's strength having marked impact on Monday's figures.

"We are expecting a further drop in input prices and a very modest incease in output prices -- up 0.1 percent on the month -- emphasising the impact of the strong pound on pipeline inflation pressures," Edmonds said.
